About the game

What is Block Blast!?

Block Blast! is a block puzzle game from Hungry Studio built around one beautifully simple idea: you are given three block pieces at a time, and you drag them onto an 8×8 board. Fill an entire row or column and it clears in a satisfying burst, freeing up space and scoring points. There is no timer and no falling pieces rushing you — the pressure comes entirely from the board slowly filling up.

What turns that simple loop into a phenomenon is the scoring. Clear more than one line with a single piece and you trigger a combo; clear lines with back-to-back placements and you build a streak that multiplies your points. A quiet, tidy board can suddenly explode into a huge score — and one careless placement can end the run, because the game is over the moment none of your three pieces fits anywhere.

The numbers behind it are remarkable. According to AppMagic estimates, Block Blast! was the most downloaded mobile game of 2025, with roughly 356 million downloads in that year alone — around 30 million a month, ahead of giants like Roblox and Subway Surfers. It is proof that a clean, relaxing puzzle can out-draw the biggest action franchises.

Beginner guide

How to Play Block Blast!

Block Blast! looks like a quiet little puzzle, and for the first minute it is. Then the board tightens, the pieces stop cooperating, and you understand why hundreds of millions of people keep coming back. This guide walks you through everything a new player needs: the board, the pieces, how lines clear, and the combo and streak systems where the big scores live.

The board and your three pieces

Every run starts on an empty 8×8 board. Below it sit three block pieces in shapes you will quickly recognise — straight bars, squares, L and T shapes, small corners and single blocks. You must place all three before a new set of three appears. There is no rotating pieces and no timer: the only question is where each shape fits best.

Placing blocks

  1. Drag a piece from the tray onto the board (on this site's mini demo, tap to select, then tap a square). A preview shows exactly where it will land.
  2. Release to place it. Once a piece is down, it cannot be moved, so look before you drop.
  3. Place all three pieces to receive the next set. Plan the set as a group — the order you place them in often decides whether they all fit.

Clearing lines

When every square in a row or a column is filled, that line clears and the blocks burst away, scoring points and freeing space. One placement can finish a row and a column at the same time if the piece sits at their crossing point — always look for those double-duty spots.

Combos and streaks: where the points are

Two scoring systems reward clever play:

  • Combo: clear two or more lines with a single placement. A combo pays far more than the same lines cleared separately, so it is worth building a position where one piece finishes several lines at once.
  • Streak: clear at least one line with consecutive placements. Each clearing placement in a row raises your streak, and the bonus grows with it. One placement that clears nothing breaks the streak — which is why good players keep a "safe" nearly-complete line in reserve.

Ordinary placements score a little; combos and streaks score a lot. Almost every high-score strategy in our Tips & Tricks comes down to feeding these two systems.

When the game ends

A run ends when none of your remaining pieces fits anywhere on the board. Pieces grey out when they have no legal spot. It rarely happens suddenly — usually you can feel it coming a few sets ahead, as awkward shapes leave single-square holes and jagged edges that nothing fits into. Keeping the board smooth and open is the whole game.

Adventure and daily play

Alongside the endless classic mode, Block Blast! offers structured content such as journey-style levels with set goals and daily puzzles. These are great training: they teach you piece shapes and clearing patterns in small, winnable doses before you chase a personal best in the endless mode.

Your first five games

  1. Game one: just place pieces and watch how lines clear. No strategy yet.
  2. Game two: start building from one corner instead of the middle.
  3. Game three: try to finish a row and a column with the same piece.
  4. Game four: keep one nearly-full line untouched as streak insurance.
  5. Game five: before each set of three, decide the order you will place them in.

Then head to our Tips & Tricks to turn those habits into real high scores — and grab the game free from the official Google Play page or the official App Store page.

Strategy

Block Blast! Tips & Tricks for High Scores

Everyone's first games end the same way: a board full of holes and a 3×3 square with nowhere to go. High scores are not about luck with pieces — the same shapes appear for everyone. They come from a handful of habits that keep your board open and your combos fed. Here are the ones that matter most.

1Build from the corners

Start each run by filling a corner and working outward along the edges. Corners and edges are the hardest places to fill later because so few pieces have the right profile for them. A board built from the corners stays flat and open in the middle, where big awkward pieces need room.

2Protect your open space

Your most valuable asset is a clear area big enough for a 3×3 square — the largest piece in the game. Before every placement, glance at the board and ask: "If the big square appears next, where does it go?" If the honest answer is "nowhere", your next move should fix that, even if it scores nothing.

3Set up combos, don't stumble into them

A combo — two or more lines cleared by one piece — is the biggest single-play score in the game. Build toward it deliberately: bring a row and a column (or two rows) to within one piece of completion, with the gap shaped like a piece you actually hold. It takes patience to leave a nearly-full line un-cleared for a turn or two, but the payoff is worth several ordinary clears.

4Keep a streak insurance line

Streaks break the moment a placement clears nothing. Keep one line a single block away from complete at all times. When a set of pieces offers nothing that clears, spend your smallest piece on the insurance line, bank the clear, and keep the streak — and its growing bonus — alive.

5Never leave single-square holes

An isolated empty square surrounded by blocks can only be filled by the rare single block. Two or three of these holes will quietly strangle a run. Fill gaps while they are still part of an open edge, and prefer placements that leave smooth, straight borders over jagged ones.

6Place the hardest piece first

When a new set of three arrives, find a home for the most awkward shape first — the big square, the long bar, the clumsy corner. Easy pieces fit anywhere; awkward ones do not. Players who place the fun pieces first are the ones staring at an unplaceable leftover at the end of the set.

7Think in whole sets of three

You always know all three pieces before you must place any of them. Use that. Decide the full sequence — where each piece goes and which line the sequence clears — before placing the first one. Mid-set surprises almost always come from placing piece one somewhere piece three needed.

8Know when a run is dying

If the board has no 3×3 space, two or more single holes, and no line within two blocks of clearing, the run is on borrowed time. Switch to survival mode: clear anything you can, anywhere you can, and stop setting up combos. Many personal bests are rescued runs that survived three ugly sets until kind pieces arrived.

Put together — corners first, open space protected, combos set up on purpose, streak insured — these habits are the entire difference between a 2,000-point player and a 20,000-point player. For the rules underneath them, revisit How to Play.

How to Get a High Score in Block Blast

Every Block Blast! player knows the feeling: one run flows beautifully and the score climbs past anything you have managed before, while the next run collapses at a few hundred points with a board full of awkward gaps. The difference is rarely luck. The same pieces appear for everyone — high scores come from how you plan placements, how jealously you protect open space, and how often you clear more than one line at a time. This article breaks the whole approach down, move by move.

Plan the set, not the piece

The single biggest jump in most players' scores comes from one habit: stop thinking piece by piece. You are always shown three pieces before you must place any of them, and that preview is a gift. Before placing the first piece, decide where all three will go and which line the set will clear. Ask three questions: Which piece is hardest to place? Where does it go? And after all three are down, what does the board look like?

Placing the hardest piece first — usually the 3×3 square, a long bar, or a chunky corner shape — guarantees it gets the room it needs while the board is still open. The easy pieces, like a straight bar or a single block, can squeeze into whatever space remains. Players who place pieces in the order they happen to tap them routinely end a set holding one piece that fits nowhere, which is exactly how runs end.

Keep space like it is money

Open space is the resource everything else depends on. A tidy board with one large open area can absorb almost any piece the game deals; a board scattered with bumps and notches can be killed by a single 3×3 square. Two rules keep your space healthy:

  • Always keep a 3×3 landing zone. Before every placement, check that a clear 3×3 area still exists somewhere. If a move would destroy your last one, find a different move — even a scoreless one.
  • Keep edges straight. A flat surface accepts bars, squares and corners alike. A jagged surface accepts almost nothing. When you have a choice, place pieces so the boundary of your filled area stays smooth and level.

Build from the corners and edges inward. Corners are the hardest spots to fill late in a run because so few pieces have the right profile, so claim them early while you still have flexible shapes, and let the roomy middle stay open for the big pieces.

Clear multiple lines, on purpose

Ordinary single-line clears keep you alive; multi-line clears make you rich. A placement that completes two, three or four lines at once triggers a combo worth far more than the same lines cleared one at a time — and it frees a huge amount of space in a single move. The way to earn combos regularly is to build toward them deliberately:

  1. Pick a target: a row and a column that cross, or two neighbouring rows.
  2. Bring both lines to within a few blocks of complete, leaving a gap shaped like a common piece — an L, a corner or a short bar.
  3. Play your other pieces elsewhere while you wait for the matching shape. Patience here is the whole skill.
  4. When the piece arrives, drop it into the crossing point and collect the combo.

The hardest part is resisting the urge to clear a nearly-full line immediately for a small, safe reward. A line left one block short is not a missed clear — it is half of a future combo. High scorers treat almost-complete lines as savings accounts, not loose change.

Feed the streak while you build

Combos are only half the scoring engine. Clearing at least one line with consecutive placements builds a streak, and the streak bonus grows the longer it runs. The trick is to combine both systems: while you are setting up a combo in one part of the board, keep a separate, easy line elsewhere that you can clear cheaply whenever a set of pieces offers nothing better. That "insurance line" keeps the streak alive during the turns you spend building, so when the combo finally lands, it lands on top of a healthy streak multiplier instead of starting from zero. Our companion article, Block Blast Combos and Streaks Explained, goes deeper into exactly how the two systems interact.

Survive the ugly sets

Even perfect play meets horrible draws: three bulky pieces in a row, nothing that clears, nowhere clean to put them. The goal in a bad set is not to score — it is to spend the set doing the least damage possible. Stack awkward pieces together in one sacrificial corner rather than scattering them across the board, keep your 3×3 zone intact if you possibly can, and clear anything, anywhere, the moment a chance appears. Most personal-best runs include two or three grim sets that were simply survived. The run that ends is usually the one where a player kept playing "normally" through a crisis and carved the board into unusable fragments.

A high-score checklist

  • Plan all three placements before placing the first piece.
  • Place the hardest piece first, while space is plentiful.
  • Never give up your last clear 3×3 area.
  • Build corners and edges early; keep surfaces flat.
  • Leave near-complete lines unfinished when a combo is one piece away.
  • Keep an insurance line so the streak survives quiet sets.
  • In a bad set, sacrifice one corner and protect everything else.

None of this requires fast fingers or luck — just a few seconds of thought before each placement. Put it together and the scores follow. If your runs still end early, read Common Beginner Mistakes in Block Blast and check whether one of those habits is quietly undoing your good play, and keep our Tips & Tricks page bookmarked for the short version.

Block Blast Combos and Streaks Explained

Two players can clear the same number of lines in a run and finish with wildly different scores. The gap is almost always explained by two words: combos and streaks. They are the twin engines of Block Blast! scoring, they reward completely different habits, and the biggest scores come from running both at once. Here is how each system works, what it pays for, and how to keep them alive.

What is a combo?

A combo happens when one placed piece completes two or more lines at the same time — two rows, two columns, or a row and a column crossing at the piece you just dropped. The game celebrates it because it is genuinely the hardest thing to engineer on the board: both lines must be built up in parallel, kept unfinished, and then completed by a single shape landing in exactly the right spot.

Combos pay a bonus well beyond the value of the lines themselves, and the bonus grows steeply with the number of lines. A two-line combo is worth noticeably more than two separate clears; a three- or four-line combo — rare, and usually the result of several turns of patient setup — can be worth more than everything else you scored in the previous minute combined. Combos also clear a lot of board at once, which buys you breathing room exactly when a run is getting crowded.

What is a streak?

A streak is about consistency rather than spectacle. Clear at least one line with a placement, then clear again with your very next placement, and your streak grows. Each consecutive clearing placement adds to the streak, and the points for each clear grow with it. The catch is absolute: a single placement that clears nothing resets the streak to zero. There is no partial credit and no grace period.

This is why streaks change how you play even more than combos do. A player protecting a long streak stops asking "what is the best placement?" and starts asking "which placement clears a line — any line?" A humble one-line clear that extends a streak of eight is worth far more than its face value, because it keeps the bonus alive for the clears still to come.

How the two systems work together

The real magic is that combos and streaks stack. A combo clear counts as a clearing placement, so it extends your streak like any other clear — while also paying its own combo bonus on top of the streak-enhanced value of the lines. In practice this means the highest-value moments in Block Blast! look like this: a long streak running, several lines primed, and one well-shaped piece that completes three of them at once. Everything the game rewards converges in that single drop.

It also means the two systems can fight each other. Setting up a combo takes turns where you deliberately do not clear the lines you are building — and every non-clearing placement threatens your streak. Skilled players resolve the tension with geography: they build the combo in one region of the board while keeping a separate, cheap line in another region purely to spend on streak maintenance. One board, two jobs.

Keeping a streak alive

  • Keep an insurance line. Maintain one row or column that is a single block away from complete. When a set of pieces contains nothing that clears, spend your smallest piece there and bank the clear.
  • Spend small pieces on maintenance. Single blocks and short bars are streak fuel. Do not waste them filling random gaps when a clear is one block away somewhere.
  • Plan the set as a sequence. Before placing anything, identify which of your three pieces will make the set's clear, and place it first if the streak is at risk. A streak saved early in the set is safe; a clear planned for "later in the set" can be ruined by your own earlier placements.
  • Clear cheap, clear often. While learning, favour frequent single-line clears over ambitious setups. A modest streak kept alive for twenty placements outscores a brilliant combo followed by silence.

Building combos reliably

Combos stop being accidents once you build for them. The most reliable pattern is the cross: one row and one column, each missing only the square where they intersect, plus perhaps one more square each. Bring both lines along together, play elsewhere while you wait, and finish both with one corner-shaped piece at the crossing. The second pattern is parallel rows: two adjacent rows missing blocks in the same columns, completed together by one wide piece. Either way, the discipline is the same — resist clearing either line early, because a line cleared alone can never be part of a combo.

The takeaway

Think of streaks as your salary and combos as your bonus. The streak pays you steadily for the unglamorous habit of clearing something with every placement; the combo pays out in bursts when patience and setup align. Chase the bonus without protecting the salary and your score stalls; protect the salary and set up the bonus, and the big numbers arrive on their own. For the broader strategy that surrounds both systems, see How to Get a High Score in Block Blast.

Block Blast Adventure Mode: How It Works and How to Win

The classic mode of Block Blast! is an endless chase: play until the board beats you, then try to beat your own score. Adventure Mode is the other half of the game — a journey through structured levels, each with a defined goal and a finish line. It plays by the same placement rules, but it rewards a different mindset. This guide explains how Adventure Mode works and the planning habits that carry you through its tougher levels.

How Adventure Mode works

Instead of an open-ended board, each Adventure level hands you a specific objective and asks you to complete it before you run out of room — or, on many levels, before you run out of moves. Depending on the level, the goal might be to reach a target score, clear a set number of lines, or clear special blocks and collectible items sitting on the board by completing the lines that pass through them. Levels are arranged as a journey: finish one to unlock the next, with difficulty climbing as new goal types and tighter boards are introduced.

Three things make it feel different from classic mode. First, many boards do not start empty — pieces are already placed, sometimes helpfully, sometimes as obstacles you must play around. Second, the move limit changes every decision: a placement that merely "doesn't hurt" is a real cost when you only have twenty moves to reach the target. Third, success is binary. In classic mode a good run is its own reward; in Adventure Mode a level is either completed or it is not, and falling one line short with no moves left is a familiar sting.

Read the goal before you touch a piece

The most common way to lose an Adventure level is to play it like a classic run. Before your first placement, read the objective carefully and let it dictate your whole approach:

  • Target score: combos and streaks matter most. Play for multi-line clears, even if it means a slower start, because single clears rarely reach a high target within the move limit.
  • Clear special blocks or items: your real targets are the rows and columns passing through those squares. Build toward those specific lines and ignore tempting clears elsewhere unless they also help.
  • Clear a set number of lines: consistency beats spectacle. Steady single clears, protected streaks, and never wasting a move.

Plan ahead — further than feels natural

Limited moves punish improvisation. In classic mode a careless placement costs you some space; in Adventure Mode it costs you space and one of a fixed number of chances. Before each set of three pieces, work out the full sequence: where each piece goes, which line each placement clears or prepares, and what the board will look like when the set ends. If a set contains no clear at all, that is a warning sign — reposition your earlier placements in the plan so the pieces cooperate instead of merely fitting.

Also look one set beyond the current one. You cannot see the next pieces coming, but you can refuse to leave the board in a state that only one specific shape could rescue. Flexible positions — flat edges, an open area for a big piece, a line one block from complete in two different places — survive unknown future pieces. Brittle positions do not.

Spend moves like a budget

Think of your move counter as money and every placement as a purchase that should buy progress toward the goal. Three spending rules help:

  1. Every move should clear, prepare, or unblock. If a placement does none of the three, look harder — there is almost always a better square.
  2. Open the board early. On levels that start crowded, your first sets should aim at clearing the lines that free the most space, even at low scores. Room to manoeuvre is worth more in move ten than in move two.
  3. Save your flexibility for the end. Levels are usually lost in the final moves, when the board is tight and the goal is close. Reaching the endgame with a nearly-complete line in reserve and one open pocket of space is the difference between finishing and stalling one move short.

When a level beats you

It will happen, and it is useful information. Before retrying, ask which of three failures occurred: Did you run out of moves with the goal nearly reached? Then your early play was too passive — chase clears sooner. Did the board jam with moves still left? Then your placement shapes were the problem — keep edges flatter and protect an open area. Did you chase the wrong thing — a big score when the goal was specific blocks? Then the fix is simply reading the objective first next time. Retrying with a diagnosis beats retrying with hope, and most "impossible" levels fall within a few attempts once the real problem is named.

Why Adventure Mode makes you better at everything

Even if high scores are your main love, Adventure Mode is the best training ground in the game. Its goals force you to practise the exact skills classic mode rewards but never demands: clearing specific lines on purpose, planning whole sets, and valuing space under pressure. Players who work through the journey return to classic mode noticeably sharper — and usually watch their personal best climb within a few runs. For the classic-mode side of the craft, see How to Get a High Score in Block Blast.

Block Blast vs Tetris: What's the Difference?

At a glance they look like cousins: coloured blocks, lines that vanish when completed, scores that climb as you clear. But Block Blast! and Tetris ask for almost opposite skills, and players who love one often bounce off the other. This comparison breaks down the real differences — how pieces move, how scoring works, where the pressure comes from — and finishes with an honest guide to which game suits which player.

The core difference: placing versus falling

In Tetris, pieces fall. A tetromino enters at the top of a tall well and descends whether you are ready or not, speeding up as the game goes on. You slide and rotate it in mid-air, but gravity always has the final say, and the game ends when the stack reaches the top. The challenge is reaction speed under escalating pressure.

In Block Blast!, nothing falls and nothing is timed. You are given three pieces at a time and drag each one onto a flat 8×8 board wherever it fits. You cannot rotate pieces, but you can take all day deciding. The game ends not when a stack overflows but when none of your three pieces fits anywhere in the remaining space. The challenge is pure planning: every defeat is a position you built yourself, one comfortable placement at a time.

How the boards and pieces differ

  • Board: Tetris uses a narrow 10-wide, 20-tall well; Block Blast! uses a square 8×8 grid.
  • Lines: Tetris clears horizontal rows only. Block Blast! clears rows and columns, which is what makes its crossing-point combos possible.
  • Pieces: Tetris has seven four-block tetrominoes that you rotate. Block Blast! has a wider menagerie — bars of several lengths, squares up to 3×3, corners, L and T shapes, and single blocks — none of which rotate.
  • Preview: Tetris shows the next piece (modern versions show several, plus a hold slot). Block Blast! shows all three current pieces at once and nothing beyond them, so you plan a set, not a queue.

Scoring: Tetrises versus combos and streaks

Tetris scoring worships one play: the Tetris, clearing four rows at once with a long piece dropped into a prepared well. Expert play is built around keeping that well open while stacking cleanly everywhere else, with T-spins and back-to-back bonuses layered on top in modern versions. Speed multiplies everything, because higher levels score more per clear.

Block Blast! spreads its rewards across two systems. Combos pay for clearing multiple rows or columns with one placement, and streaks pay for clearing something with consecutive placements — systems explained in depth in Block Blast Combos and Streaks Explained. Where Tetris scoring peaks in rare, spectacular four-line moments, Block Blast! scoring is steadier: a long streak of modest clears can rival a big combo, and the best runs combine both.

Pace and pressure

This is the difference players feel most. Tetris is a game of escalating urgency: the longer you survive, the faster it gets, until survival itself is the achievement. Sessions are intense, and mistakes compound in seconds. Block Blast! applies no time pressure at all. You can put the phone down mid-decision and return an hour later. Its pressure is spatial and slow-burning — a board that tightens set by set until one piece has no home. One game tests your reflexes; the other tests your foresight.

Which one suits you?

Choose Tetris if you enjoy adrenaline, mastery through repetition, and the feeling of your hands getting faster than your thoughts. Its competitive scene, marathon records and split-second saves offer a very high skill ceiling for players who like intensity.

Choose Block Blast! if you want a puzzle you can think about — on a commute, in a queue, in bed — where a run is won by planning rather than reflexes, and where a two-minute session or a twenty-minute one both feel complete. Its lack of a timer makes it genuinely relaxing in a way Tetris never tries to be, while the combo and streak systems still give planners plenty to master.

Choose both if you like block puzzles generally. Many players find the skills transfer in one direction only: Tetris teaches tidy stacking and clean surfaces, which help in Block Blast!, while Block Blast! teaches patient setup and playing for the position three moves ahead — a habit that will make your Tetris stacking cleaner, if you can convince your hands to slow down. They are not rivals so much as two answers to the same question: how much fun can you get from fitting shapes into lines? Nearly forty years apart, both answers are still being played by millions.

Common Beginner Mistakes in Block Blast

Almost every Block Blast! run that ends early ends for one of a handful of reasons — and they are rarely bad luck. New players tend to make the same quiet mistakes: nothing dramatic, just small placements that feel harmless and slowly close the board like a fist. Here are the most common ones, why they hurt, and what to do instead.

Mistake 1: Sealing off the corners

Corners look like natural storage: tuck an awkward piece up against the edge and forget about it. The trouble is that a corner filled almost completely — with one or two squares left empty inside a pocket of blocks — becomes nearly impossible to finish later, because very few pieces carry the exact profile a sealed corner needs. Those stranded squares sit there for the rest of the run, breaking every row and column that passes through them. Instead: fill corners completely and deliberately, early, with pieces that match their shape, and build outward from them. A finished corner is an asset; a nearly-finished one is a trap.

Mistake 2: Ignoring the other pieces in the set

You are shown three pieces at a time for a reason, yet beginners routinely place the first piece wherever it fits and only then look at the other two. This is how a set ends with an unplaceable 3×3 square: the space it needed was given away thirty seconds earlier to a bar that would have fit in five other places. Instead: before placing anything, find a home for the hardest piece in the set, then fit the flexible pieces around that decision. Place in order of difficulty, not in order of tapping.

Mistake 3: Wasting the big pieces — and fearing them

The 3×3 square provokes two opposite errors. Some players drop it into the first open space they see, in the middle of the board, where it fragments the open area into strips too narrow for anything else. Others dread it and postpone it, filling the very space it needed with smaller pieces until it fits nowhere and the run ends with the square still in the tray. Instead: treat the big square as a first-class citizen. Keep a 3×3 landing zone open at all times, and when the square arrives, place it promptly — against an edge or in a corner region, where it consumes space you value least.

Mistake 4: Chasing every clear immediately

Clearing a line feels like progress, so beginners clear every line the moment it completes. But a line cleared alone pays the smallest possible reward and can destroy a combo that was one placement away: bring a row and a column to near-completion and one piece could have cleared both, with a combo bonus on top. Instead: when a second line is close behind the first, wait. Leave the nearly-full line untouched for a set or two, finish building its partner, and take both together. The exception is streak protection — if a clear is needed this placement to keep a streak alive, take the clear and rebuild the combo later.

Mistake 5: Leaving single-square holes

An isolated empty square surrounded on all sides by blocks can only ever be filled by the single-block piece, one of the rarest shapes in the game. One hole is an annoyance; three holes quietly guarantee that several rows and columns can never clear, and the board strangles around them. Instead: fill gaps while they are still part of an open edge, and prefer placements that leave straight borders. When you must leave a gap, leave it in a line that is otherwise nearly complete, so a clear will erase it soon.

Mistake 6: Playing in the middle

Beginners gravitate to the centre of the board because everything fits there — at first. A blob in the middle splits the board into four small quadrants, none of which can hold a big piece, and leaves all four corners to be filled by shapes that rarely cooperate. Instead: work from one corner along the edges, keeping the middle open as long as possible. The centre is your reserve space, not your building site.

Mistake 7: Never looking at the streak

Many new players do not realise a streak exists until they notice the score jumping. Then they lose it constantly, because nothing in their placement choices protects it — sets go by with no clear at all while they build pretty patterns. Instead: keep one line a single block from complete at all times as insurance, and make sure every set of three contains at least one clearing placement, even a cheap one. A modest streak defended for twenty placements is worth more than most combos; our combos and streaks article shows the maths of why.

The encouraging part

Every mistake on this list is a habit, not a talent gap — and habits can be replaced in a handful of games. Pick one fix at a time: play five runs doing nothing new except placing the hardest piece first, then five protecting your corners, and so on. Most players who work through the list watch their average score climb within a day or two, because the pieces were never the problem. For the positive version of all this advice — what to do, not just what to avoid — read How to Get a High Score in Block Blast next.

Best Opening Moves in Block Blast

The board is empty, three fresh pieces are waiting, and anything feels possible. That feeling is exactly why the opening matters so much. The first placements in Block Blast! do not score many points, but they decide the shape of everything that follows — whether your board stays open and flexible for twenty minutes, or slowly closes into corners and holes you cannot fix. This guide shows how strong players start, and why keeping the centre open is the habit that changes everything.

Why the first placements shape the whole board

Block Blast! has no timer, so it is tempting to treat early moves as warm-ups and drop pieces wherever they fit. The problem is that early pieces become the foundation. A bar placed casually across the middle splits the board into smaller pockets. A square tucked into the centre leaves four narrow strips around it, none of them wide enough for a big piece later. By contrast, a tidy opening along one edge leaves you with one large, continuous space — and large continuous space is what lets you survive awkward draws later in the run.

Think of the opening as drawing the map for the rest of the game. You are not just placing three pieces; you are choosing where future pieces will be allowed to go.

Start in a corner, then work along the edge

The most reliable opening is also the simplest: claim one corner completely and build outward along the two edges that meet there. Corners are the hardest places to fill in the late game because so few pieces have the right profile for a tight corner pocket. Filling a corner early, while you still have small and flexible shapes, removes that problem before it starts.

  1. Pick a corner — bottom-left and bottom-right are popular because they feel natural to build from.
  2. Place your first piece so one of its sides sits flush against the edge, with no single-square gap left behind it.
  3. Use the next pieces to extend along the bottom and side edges, keeping the outer boundary straight.
  4. Only move inward once the corner region is solid and flat on its inner side.

The result should look like a neat staircase or a clean block growing from the corner — not a scattered pattern. If your first three pieces end up in three different areas of the board, you have not started a run; you have started three small problems.

Keep the centre open on purpose

If there is one rule in this article worth remembering, it is this: protect the centre. The middle of the 8×8 board is the only area large enough to comfortably receive the biggest pieces — especially the 3×3 square — from almost any direction. Once the centre is occupied by an early piece, every later big piece must be squeezed toward an edge, and edges run out quickly.

Keeping the centre open does not mean leaving a perfect empty square forever. It means checking, before every early placement, that a clear 3×3 area still exists somewhere in the middle band of the board. Place around it, not in it, for as long as you can. When a 3×3 piece finally arrives — and it will — you will be grateful for the patience.

  • Prefer edge placements over central ones in the first three sets, even when the central spot looks tidy.
  • If you must play toward the middle, keep the placement flat against your existing blocks so it does not create a bump.
  • Count the open space: if you cannot picture the 3×3 square landing somewhere, your next move should reopen space, not score points.

Build flat edges, not interesting shapes

Good openings are boring to look at, and that is a compliment. A flat surface accepts almost anything: bars lie along it, squares sit on it, corners notch into its end. A jagged surface with bumps and notches accepts almost nothing, because most pieces are regular shapes that need a straight run of two, three or four squares.

When you have a choice between two placements, choose the one that leaves the straighter border. Put the taller part of an L-shape against the wall and the short part pointing inward only if it keeps the line level. Fill dips before you build peaks. This habit feels fussy for the first few games and then becomes automatic — and it is the same habit that prevents the single-square holes described in Common Beginner Mistakes in Block Blast.

Plan the first three sets as one opening

Strong players do not just plan the current set of three pieces — in the opening, they plan an intention for the first three sets: for example, "fill the bottom two rows from the left, keep the centre empty, and leave the top-right corner for later." You cannot know which pieces are coming, but you can hold a direction. A direction stops you from reacting randomly to each new set and slowly drifting into the middle.

Within each set, still place the hardest piece first. In the opening that usually means the largest piece goes against the edge first, while there is unlimited room, and the small pieces tidy up around it. Small pieces are flexible; they will fit in the gaps your plan leaves. Big pieces are not flexible at all.

What a good opening looks like after ten placements

You do not need a perfect pattern, but a healthy board after roughly ten placements usually has four features: one or two corners fully claimed, a mostly flat filled region hugging one or two edges, a clear central area of at least 3×3, and no isolated single-square holes. Lines may not have cleared yet, and that is fine — the opening is about position, not points. The clears and combos come easily on a board shaped like this, because almost any line you choose to build toward has room to be finished.

If your board instead looks busy in the middle and empty at the edges, do not panic. Spend the next few sets moving your play outward, clearing any line that touches the centre, and restoring one large open area. Openings can be rescued — but it is far easier to start well. Combine this start with the scoring ideas in How to Get a High Score in Block Blast and your whole run, not just its first minute, will feel calmer and last longer.

How to Clear the Entire Board in Block Blast

There is one moment in Block Blast! that players talk about the way anglers talk about the one that got away: the full-board clear, when the last placement completes the final lines and every single block on the 8×8 board bursts away, leaving it completely empty. It is rare, it is not required to score well, and chasing it carelessly will end more runs than it crowns. But with the right setup, a little piece saving, and an eye for the moment, it is achievable — and unforgettable. Here is how it actually happens.

What a full-board clear really requires

An empty board after a clear means that every filled square on the board belonged to a row or column that was completed by your final placement. In practice, that final piece usually completes several lines at once — the last row and the last column, crossing at the piece — and those lines between them must cover every block still on the board. There can be no stray block sitting in a line that does not complete. That single condition explains both the beauty and the difficulty: for many turns before the finish, you must build a board where every block is part of a nearly-complete line.

This is why a full-board clear is an endgame project, not an opening plan. Early in a run the board is too empty for the idea to mean anything. It becomes realistic in the middle and late game, when you can look at the board and honestly say: most of what is here is already organised into lines that are one or two pieces away from done.

Setting up: build a board of almost-lines

The setup phase is about discipline. Instead of clearing lines as soon as they complete — the habit that serves you well in ordinary high-score play — you deliberately bring many lines to the edge of completion and leave them there, while making sure no block exists outside those lines.

  1. Choose your finishing corner. Pick one corner region where the final lines will cross. Most full-board clears finish with a row and a column completed by one piece near a corner or edge.
  2. Fill in rows and columns, not patches. Every placement should extend an existing row or column. If a piece would leave blocks in a line you are not planning to complete, place it somewhere else or rethink the plan.
  3. Keep a count. Mentally track how many squares each unfinished line still needs. A setup is healthy when most lines need only one small piece, and unhealthy when several lines each need a different awkward shape.
  4. Protect one open lane. You still need somewhere to place pieces you are forced to play while waiting. Keep one row or column as your working lane and plan to complete it last.

Throughout the setup, the rule from normal play still applies: never leave single-square holes. A single isolated empty square in the middle of a line you cannot finish is the most common reason an otherwise perfect setup collapses.

Piece saving: holding the right shape for the finish

You cannot store pieces in Block Blast! — the three pieces in your tray must all be placed before new ones arrive. "Saving" a piece therefore means something subtler: arranging your placements so that the piece you need for the finish is the last one you are forced to use, and shaping the gaps so that a common piece can do the final job.

Design the finish around shapes the game gives often — a corner piece, a short bar, a 2×2 square — rather than hoping for one exact rare shape. If your setup can only be finished by a single specific piece in a single specific orientation, it is not a setup; it is a lottery ticket. Good setups have two or three acceptable finishing pieces. Within a set, place the pieces that do not finish anything first, in your working lane, and keep the potential finisher for last, once the board is exactly ready for it.

Also save space, not just pieces. The finishing piece needs its squares empty and connected in the right shape. Guard that footprint jealously in the final sets, even if it means placing another piece in a slightly worse spot elsewhere.

Recognising the moment

The moment announces itself if you know what to look for. Pause before placing anything and ask three questions:

  • Can I name the exact lines that will complete on the final placement?
  • Is every block currently on the board part of one of those lines?
  • Do I hold, in this set, a piece that fills the remaining gaps of those lines at once?

Three yeses mean go — and go now, because the next set may force you to spoil the position. Two yeses mean you are close: identify the one stray block or the one unfinished line and make removing it your only goal for the next set or two. One yes means it is still a dream; return to ordinary play, keep your streak alive with the methods in Block Blast Combos and Streaks Explained, and let the position develop.

There is also a moment to abandon the attempt, and recognising it matters just as much. If holding the setup forces you to refuse clears for several sets while the board fills dangerously, cash out: take the biggest combo available, enjoy the points, and live to play on. A four-line combo banked is worth far more than a full-board clear that ends the run one piece short.

After the clear: the sweetest fresh start in the game

When it lands, enjoy it — the board wipes clean, the bonus lands, and you get something no other play in Block Blast! gives you: a completely fresh board in the middle of a run, with your score and momentum intact. Treat the next sets exactly like an opening: corners first, centre protected, flat edges. Many players, still buzzing, play loosely for a few sets and give the advantage straight back. The best follow-up to a full-board clear is the discipline of our Best Opening Moves guide, played all over again.

You may go many sessions between full-board clears, and that is normal — they are the game's rarest celebration, not a quota. Set up honestly, save the flexible pieces, watch for the three yeses, and when the moment comes, you will know.

Games Like Block Blast: 7 Relaxing Block Puzzle Games

So Block Blast! has taken over your coffee breaks, your commute and possibly your dreams — and now you want more of the same feeling: no timers shouting at you, no opponents, just shapes, space and the quiet satisfaction of a line completed. The good news is that drag-and-place and block puzzles are a whole family, and each member has its own personality. Here are seven games like Block Blast!, what makes each one different, and who each one suits best. All of them are free to start on Android and iPhone, supported by ads or optional purchases.

1. Woodoku

Woodoku takes the drag-and-place idea and carves it out of wood. You place wooden pieces on a 9×9 board and clear by completing rows, columns and 3×3 boxes — a blend of block puzzle and Sudoku thinking. The warm wooden look and gentle sounds make it one of the most relaxing games in this list.

Best for: players who like Block Blast! but want a slightly more thoughtful, Sudoku-flavoured board, and anyone who finds bright colours tiring. If you enjoy planning around boxes as well as lines, start here.

2. Blockudoku

Blockudoku is Woodoku's close cousin with a cleaner, brighter style: the same 9×9 board, the same mix of lines and 3×3 squares to complete, plus combo and streak scoring that will feel instantly familiar to Block Blast! players. Daily challenges and events give it a little more structure than most games here.

Best for: Block Blast! fans who want the closest possible experience with one extra layer — the 3×3 box — and players who like a daily goal to come back to.

3. 1010! Block Puzzle

One of the originals of the genre. 1010! gives you three pieces at a time on a 10×10 board, with rows and columns to complete and no timer. It is plainer than Block Blast! — no streak system, simpler presentation — but that simplicity is its charm, and games can stretch into long, meditative sessions.

Best for: purists. If you love the core placing-and-clearing loop and do not need combos, characters or events around it, 1010! is the distilled version.

4. Block Puzzle (Jewel Block Puzzle)

This family of jewel-themed block puzzles keeps the 8×8 or 10×10 drag-and-place rules but wraps them in gems, sparkle effects and satisfying shattering clears. The gameplay will feel like home within a minute; the presentation is for players who find plain blocks a little dry.

Best for: players who enjoy match-3 style sparkle and sound, and younger players who are drawn in by colour and effects while they learn spatial planning.

5. Wood Block Puzzle

Wood Block Puzzle strips the idea back to basics on a wooden board: place the pieces, complete lines, survive as long as you can. There are fewer extra modes and less decoration than in Woodoku, which makes it light, fast to open and easy on older phones.

Best for: anyone who wants a small, simple, no-fuss block puzzle for quick sessions, or a first block puzzle for a less tech-confident family member.

6. Tetris

The ancestor of them all, and the one game here that is not relaxing in the same way: pieces fall, speed rises, and your hands must keep up with your brain. We compare the two in depth in Block Blast vs Tetris, but the short version is that Tetris trades calm for adrenaline — and millions of players consider that a great trade.

Best for: Block Blast! players who catch themselves wishing for more pace and pressure, and anyone who enjoys mastering a skill where reflexes matter as much as planning.

7. Hexa Block Puzzle

Hexa puzzles swap the square grid for honeycomb hexagons: you drag clusters of hex pieces onto a hexagonal board and complete lines in three directions instead of two. It sounds like a small change and plays like a genuinely different brain-teaser, because shapes fit together at angles your square-trained eye is not used to.

Best for: experienced block puzzlers who feel they have "solved" the square board and want their spatial thinking stretched in a new direction, without any added speed or stress.

How to choose your next puzzle

If you want the nearest neighbour to Block Blast!, choose Blockudoku or Woodoku. If you want the idea at its purest, choose 1010! or Wood Block Puzzle. If presentation is half the pleasure, choose the jewel-style Block Puzzle. If you want more energy, choose Tetris; if you want a fresh kind of thinking at the same calm pace, choose a Hexa puzzle. And there is no rule that says you must move on at all — many players keep Block Blast! as their main game and keep one alternative installed for the days when a different board just sounds nice. Whichever you pick, the skills travel with you: corners first, edges flat, centre protected, and never, ever leave a single-square hole.

About This Site & the Game

About Block Blast!

Block Blast! is a block puzzle game developed by Hungry Studio. Players drag colourful block pieces onto an 8×8 board, complete rows and columns to clear them, and chase ever-higher scores through combos and streaks. Released in 2022, it grew quietly for two years before becoming a global phenomenon: AppMagic estimates it was the most downloaded mobile game of 2025, with about 356 million downloads that year — roughly 30 million a month.

Its appeal is easy to understand. A game takes two minutes or twenty. There is no energy system forcing you to wait, no opponent, no timer — just a board, three pieces, and your own planning. It plays offline, runs on modest phones, and suits every age that can drag a shape across a screen.

About this website

This is an unofficial, fan-made information site created to help players discover the game, learn its rules and improve their scores. We write all of our guides and articles ourselves. We are not Hungry Studio, we do not distribute the game, and every download button on this site leads to the game's official Google Play or Apple App Store page. Read our full Disclaimer for the details.

What you will find here

  • A beginner-friendly How to Play guide covering pieces, lines, combos and streaks.
  • Original Tips & Tricks for higher scores, from corner play to combo setup.
  • An honest FAQ covering price, offline play, download size, kids and PC play.
  • A small playable board demo on the home page so you can feel the rules before downloading.
